The deflection is proportional to the current **through the galvanometer**, so the drop
from 100 divisions to 1 tells us how the shunt has divided the current.
**Step 1 — interpret the deflections.** Deflection ∝ I_g, so the galvanometer now carries
I_g = I/100 ✓
one hundredth of the main current.
**Step 2 — apply the current-divider rule.** With the shunt S in parallel with the
galvanometer G,
I_g/I = S/(S + G)
**Step 3 — substitute.**
1/100 = 1/(1 + G)
**Step 4 — solve.**
1 + G = 100
**G = 99 Ω** ✓
**A check on the division.** With G = 99 Ω and S = 1 Ω, the currents divide in inverse
proportion:
galvanometer : shunt = 1 : 99 ✓
so the galvanometer takes 1 part in 100 - exactly the hundredfold reduction observed.
**Why the main current stays the same.** The question's phrasing assumes the same current
reaches the combination both times ✓ In practice the parallel pair has a lower
resistance than the galvanometer alone, so the main current would rise slightly; the
problem treats the source as supplying a fixed current.
**The general result.** To reduce a deflection by a factor n with a shunt S,
**G = (n − 1)S** ✓
Here n = 100 and S = 1 Ω, giving 99 Ω directly.
**Why this is a practical method.** It measures the galvanometer's own resistance using
nothing but a known shunt and two deflection readings ✓ No separate ohmmeter is
needed - this is the **half-deflection** method in a more extreme form, where n = 2 gives
the familiar G = S.
**Reading the distractors.** **100 Ω** ✗ forgets the "−1", a very near miss and the
commonest answer. **10 Ω** ✗ and **9·9 Ω** ✗ correspond to deflection ratios of 11 and
10·9, not 100 ✓
∴ 99 Ω.

Separating the loops reduces the flux each sends through the other, and by **Lenz's law**
the circuits respond by trying to keep that flux up.
**Step 1 — note the initial state.** The currents circulate in the **same** direction, so
each loop's field threads the other in the **same** sense ✓ The two are mutually linked,
and each adds to the flux through the other.
**Step 2 — see what moving them apart does.** The mutual inductance M falls with
distance, so the flux each loop receives from the other **decreases** ✓
**Step 3 — apply Lenz's law.** The induced emf opposes the **change**, which here is a
**decrease** in flux ✓ So each loop develops an emf that tries to **maintain** the flux -
that is, to **increase** its own current.
**Step 4 — conclude.** The current **increases in both** loops ✓
**Why both, and not one of each.** The situation is completely **symmetric** ✓ Each loop
sees the other's flux falling in the same way, so each responds identically. Nothing
distinguishes one from the other.
**The force between them.** Parallel currents in the same direction **attract** ✓ so
pulling the loops apart is done against that attraction, and the work done goes into the
extra magnetic energy of the strengthened currents - which is the energy bookkeeping
behind Lenz's law.
**The companion case.** Had the currents been in **opposite** directions, the mutual flux
would be negative, and separating the loops would cause the currents to **decrease** in
both ✓ The direction of the response always follows from "oppose the change".
**Why the effect is temporary.** The induced emf lasts only while the loops are
**moving** ✓ Once they come to rest at the new separation, the flux stops changing and
the currents settle back to whatever the sources dictate.
**Reading the distractors.** **Decrease in both** ✗ reverses Lenz's law. **Remain
unaltered** ✗ would require no change of flux, contradicting the movement. **Increases
in one, decreases in the other** ✗ breaks the symmetry of the arrangement ✓
∴ increase in both.

A flat spiral is a stack of circular turns of **every** radius between a and b, so the
contributions must be **integrated**, not simply multiplied.
**Step 1 — write the field of one turn.** A single circular turn of radius r carrying
current I gives, at its centre,
dB = μ₀I/(2r) ✓
**Step 2 — count the turns in a thin ring.** The n turns are spread uniformly across the
radial width (b − a), so the number in a ring of thickness dr is
dN = n dr/(b − a) ✓
**Step 3 — assemble the integral.**
B = ∫ₐᵇ [μ₀I/(2r)] x [n dr/(b − a)]
= [μ₀nI/(2(b − a))] ∫ₐᵇ dr/r
**Step 4 — integrate.**
∫ₐᵇ dr/r = **ln(b/a)**
so
**B = [μ₀nI/(2(b − a))] ln(b/a)** ✓
**Why the logarithm appears.** The inner turns, being smaller, contribute far more field
than the outer ones - the 1/r weighting ✓ Integrating 1/r always produces a logarithm,
and that is the signature of this geometry.
**A check on the limits.** If the spiral is thin, b = a + δ with δ small:
ln(b/a) = ln(1 + δ/a) ≈ δ/a
so B ≈ [μ₀nI/(2δ)](δ/a) = **μ₀nI/(2a)** ✓ exactly n concentric turns of radius a, as it
should be.
**A worked value.** With n = 100, I = 1 A, a = 2 cm and b = 4 cm:
B = (4π x 10⁻⁷)(100)(1)/(2 x 0·02) x ln 2
= 3·14 x 10⁻³ x 0·693
= **2·18 x 10⁻³ T** ✓
**Checking the dimensions.** μ₀nI/(b − a) has units (T m A⁻¹)(A)/m = **T** ✓ and the
logarithm is dimensionless, as it must be since b/a is a pure ratio.
**Reading the distractors.** The two options **without** a logarithm ✗ cannot be right -
integrating 1/r across a finite range must produce one. The option with **ln(a/b)** ✗ is
**negative**, since a < b, and a field magnitude cannot be ✓
∴ [μ₀nI/(2(b − a))] logₑ(b/a).

The electron's own magnetic field threads the loop, and that flux first **grows** and
then **falls** as the electron passes - so the induced current reverses.
**Step 1 — find the flux the electron produces.** A moving charge carries a magnetic
field with it. With the electron travelling along a straight line in the **plane** of the
loop, its field at every point of the loop is **perpendicular** to that plane ✓ so it
does thread the loop and the flux is not zero.
**Step 2 — see how that flux changes.** As the electron approaches, it comes closer to
the loop and the flux through it **increases** ✓ After the point of closest approach the
electron recedes and the flux **decreases**.
**Step 3 — apply Lenz's law to each stage.**
while the flux **grows**, the induced current opposes it and flows one way
while the flux **falls**, the induced current reverses to oppose the decrease ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** The induced current is not steadily clockwise or anticlockwise; it
flows one way, dies to zero at closest approach, and then flows the other way. Its
direction and magnitude both change with time - the current is **variable** ✓
**Why it is not zero.** Zero would require the flux through the loop to stay constant ✓
It does not: the electron's field at the loop depends on its distance, which is changing
throughout.
**Why neither single direction can be right.** Both occur, at different stages of the
passage ✓ Naming only one would describe just half the event.
**What happens at closest approach.** The flux is at its **maximum**, so dΦ/dt = 0 and
the induced current momentarily **vanishes** before reversing ✓ That instant is the
turning point of the whole process.
**The energy involved.** Whichever way it flows, the induced current creates a field that
**opposes** the electron's motion - resisting its approach and then resisting its
departure ✓ The electron loses a little kinetic energy, which appears as heat in the
loop, exactly as conservation of energy requires.
**Reading the distractors.** **Clockwise** ✗ and **anticlockwise** ✗ each describe only
one half of the passage. **Zero** ✗ would need a constant flux ✓
∴ variable.

The magnetic dipole moment is a property of the **loop and its current alone**, not of
where the loop happens to be.
**Step 1 — write the definition.**
**m = nIA** ✓
where n is the number of turns, I the current and A the area enclosed.
**Step 2 — check each option against it.**
**number of turns** ✗ appears explicitly - doubling n doubles m
**area of the loop** ✗ appears explicitly - a wider loop has a larger moment
**current in the loop** ✗ appears explicitly
**the external magnetic field** ✓ does **not** appear at all
**Step 3 — conclude.** The dipole moment is **independent of the magnetic field in which
the loop lies** ✓
**What the external field does affect.** Not m itself, but what happens to the loop:
**torque**: τ̄ = m̄ x B̄, greatest when the loop's plane contains B ✓
**potential energy**: U = −m̄·B̄, lowest when m̄ is aligned with B̄
Both involve B, but both also need m, which the loop carries in its own right.
**The analogy with electricity.** An electric dipole has moment p = qd, fixed by the
charges and their separation ✓ Placing it in a field produces a torque p̄ x Ē, but does
not change p. A current loop behaves identically.
**A worked value.** A 100-turn coil of radius 5 cm carrying 2 A:
A = π(0·05)² = **7·85 x 10⁻³ m²**
m = 100 x 2 x 7·85 x 10⁻³ = **1·57 A m²** ✓
the same number whether the coil sits in a laboratory magnet or in free space.
**The one caveat.** If the loop is made of a **magnetic material**, a strong external
field can magnetise it and add a contribution ✓ For an ordinary current loop of copper
wire, which is what the question means, m = nIA is the whole of it.
**Why the direction is given by the right-hand rule.** Curl the fingers along the
current and the thumb gives m̄, perpendicular to the loop's plane ✓ Again, the external
field plays no part in fixing it.
∴ magnetic field in which it is lying.

With the battery straight across the 3 Ω resistor, that resistor sees the full 3 V
regardless of the rest of the circuit.
**Step 1 — see the topology.** The three resistors form a triangle, and the battery is
connected across the 3 Ω side ✓ So the 3 Ω resistor is directly in parallel with the
battery, and the 1 Ω and 2 Ω in series form the other path between the same two points.
**Step 2 — find the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor.** The battery has negligible
internal resistance, so the full emf appears across it:
**V = 3 V** ✓
**Step 3 — apply Ohm's law to that branch alone.**
I = V/R
= 3/3
= **1 A** ✓
**Why the other two resistors do not matter.** They form a **separate** parallel branch ✓
Whatever current they draw comes from the battery, not from the 3 Ω resistor, and the
voltage across the 3 Ω is fixed by the battery itself.
**The current in the other branch, for completeness.**
I₂ = 3/(1 + 2) = **1 A** as well
so the battery supplies **2 A** in total ✓ The two branches happen to have equal
resistance, 3 Ω each, so they share the current equally.
**The equivalent resistance seen by the battery.**
R_eq = (3 x 3)/(3 + 3) = **1·5 Ω**
and a check: I_total = 3/1·5 = **2 A** ✓ consistent with the branch currents.
**Why "negligible internal resistance" matters.** It guarantees that the terminal
voltage equals the emf ✓ With a real internal resistance r, the voltage across the 3 Ω
would be 3 x 1·5/(1·5 + r), slightly less, and the current correspondingly smaller.
**The general lesson.** When a component is connected **directly across** an ideal
source, its current depends only on its own resistance ✓ The rest of the network is
irrelevant to it.
**Reading the distractors.** **2 A** ✗ is the **total** current drawn from the battery.
**1·5 A** ✗ is the equivalent resistance read as a current, and **0·75 A** ✗ would need
4 Ω across 3 V ✓
∴ 1 A.

A **potentiometer** measures emf by a null method, drawing **no current** from the cell -
which is exactly what accuracy requires.
**Step 1 — see the difficulty with a voltmeter.** Any voltmeter draws some current I from
the cell, so it reads the **terminal voltage**
V = E − I r ✗
not the emf E ✓ The reading is always a little low, by an amount that depends on the
cell's internal resistance.
**Step 2 — see how the potentiometer avoids it.** It is balanced against a known
potential gradient until the galvanometer shows **zero deflection** ✓ At that balance
point **no current flows** through the cell, so
I = 0, and V = E − 0 = **E** exactly ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** Accurate measurement of emf requires a potentiometer ✓
**Why no current means no error.** The internal resistance only matters when current
flows through it ✓ At null, the cell is doing no work, nothing is dropped inside it, and
the quantity measured is the true emf.
**How the balance works.** A steady current through a long uniform wire creates a uniform
potential gradient k volts per metre ✓ The unknown cell is opposed against a length ℓ of
that wire, and at balance
**E = kℓ** ✓
so the emf is read off as a **length** - a quantity that can be measured very precisely.
**The further advantage.** A potentiometer can also compare two cells directly:
E₁/E₂ = ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ✓
and it can measure a cell's internal resistance, by balancing with and without an
external load.
**Why the other instruments fall short.**
**voltmeter** ✗ - draws current, reads terminal voltage; a high-resistance digital
voltmeter comes close but is never exact
**multimeter** ✗ - a voltmeter in another form, with the same limitation
**voltameter** ✗ - not a voltage instrument at all; it measures the **mass deposited by
electrolysis**, and so measures charge ✓ The near-identical name is the trap in this
question.
∴ potentiometer.
